title: The first translators
hookLine: An Shigao and others begin translating into Chinese in Luoyang

cards: How do you say nirvana in a language that has no word for it? That was the job waiting in Luoyang, a great Chinese capital, when monks from the west arrived with texts in their heads and on their backs.
The city had readers and writers enough. What it lacked were words: Chinese had no ready words for karma, for rebirth, for a monk's rule. Every sentence was a bridge someone had to build.

teach.b: First, a name: An Shigao. The An in his name marked him, in Chinese records, as coming from Parthia, far to the west. Tradition says he was a prince who gave the throne to an uncle and became a monk.
In Luoyang he translated texts on meditation and the breath, on counting breaths and watching the mind. Second, he wasn't alone.
Another monk, Lokakshema, from the Kushan lands, translated some of the early Mahayana sutras, and others joined them.
The work was done in teams: a foreign monk recited or read the text, someone turned it into spoken Chinese, and a Chinese scribe wrote it down and polished it. Third, the hard part: the words.
Where Chinese had no word, translators sometimes borrowed one from Chinese thought. Some used dao, the way, a word from the Chinese classics, for the Buddhist path.
Others sounded the foreign word out in Chinese syllables. Both choices had a cost.

teach.h: BORROW A WORD OR SOUND IT OUT.
teach.b: A borrowed word brought its old meanings with it, and a sounded-out word meant nothing until someone explained it.
The Chinese Buddhist texts read in China, Korea and Japan today come out of a long line of choices like these, made by people working between languages, at a table, one sentence at a time.

how: Buddhists in China, Korea and Japan read the sutras in classical Chinese translations, and teachers often explain the translators' word choices when they teach a text.

games.q: you're translating, and Chinese has no word for the Buddhist path. what do you do?
o: leave a blank in the text.
borrow a word from Chinese thought, or sound the foreign word out.
games.why: translators did both. a borrowed word like dao brought old meanings with it; a sounded-out word needed explaining.

practice: Take a simple teaching about the breath: breathing in, know that you are breathing in; breathing out, know that you are breathing out.
Say it two or three ways, as you would to a twelve-year-old or a friend at the kitchen table, and notice what each version gains and loses.
Then let the words go and rest with one breath at a time, the way An Shigao's breath texts describe it.

wordCard.voice: An Shigao. A monk from Parthia who translated texts on meditation and the breath in Luoyang, building Chinese words where none existed.

carryVoice: Your line: into Chinese. Every borrowed word carried a little of its old home. Until tomorrow.
